blocks.text: 40 Morning Prayer for the New Year 40

Thee, O King. Mayest Thou preserve grace towards the offspring of him to whom three of the King's angels were sent (Abraham). Take heed of those who approach with prayer for the sake of him whom the King's Erelim did bitterly bewail (Isaac at the sacrifice). Reject not their humility for the sake of him who lodged the night at the place where the King's angels ascended and descended (Jacob).
blocks.layout: paragraph carried over from the previous page; 'hu-/mility' is hyphenated at the line break

blocks.text: פדם
blocks.layout: Hebrew cue at the start of the paragraph

blocks.text: Redeem them this day in judgment, do not utterly condemn them, O King. Acquit them in mercy, remember them kindly, O King. Heed the sound of the blast of those who blow the Shofar before Thee this day (heed the memory of the Shofar blast of those who commemorate before Thee this day) O King. Arouse compassion towards those who hope for Thee, O King.
שעה
Turn towards the supplication of the people who seek Thee, O King, heed those who hold firmly to the blessing of Thy Name, that we may bless Thee, O living God and King.
והאופנים
The Ophanim and the holy Hayoth rise with a loud tumult opposite the Seraphim, opposite them they praise and say:
Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place.
לאל

To God, who is blessed, they offer pleasant songs, to the King, the living eternal God, they intone songs of praise and let words of praise be heard. For He alone achieves mighty deeds, creates new things, dominates wars, sows kindnesses, lets salvation spring forth, creates remedies, He is awe-inspiring in deeds of renown, Lord of wonders, who daily in His goodness constantly renews the work of creation. As it says: To the Creator of the great lights, His mercy endures for ever. Let a new light shine forth over Zion that we may all soon be worthy of its light. Blessed art Thou, O Lord, who creates the lights.

observations: Both pages start in the middle of the Ofan piyyut: the Hebrew opens with the tail word מֶלֶךְ׃ and the English opens with 'Thee, O King.'
The English has no separate cue for the נָא stanza; it runs on in the carried-over paragraph. The Hebrew runs on the same way.
The English parenthetical '(heed the memory ... this day)' translates only the בשבת variant. The וי״א variant has no English rendering.
The English uses bracketed glosses (Abraham), (Isaac at the sacrifice), (Jacob). These are part of the printed English text.
The divine Name is printed as the abbreviation יְיָ (in כְּבוֹד־יְיָ and בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה יְיָ).
Several letters are stretched to fill out lines: א in אֵילֵי, ה in לְטוֹבָה, and the large ל of לךְ.
I stopped before Ahavah Rabbah, which starts at אַהֲבָה רַבָּה on s108 and the cue אהבה on s109. I didn't transcribe it.
